strengths: The separation rule (gcse-maths-marker/SKILL.md:80-82; gcse-spanish-marker/SKILL.md:152-155) keeps every answer out of the student file, so re-working a lost question is genuine retrieval practice rather than copying. Keep it exactly as strict.

Hints in the maths example are mostly method-level and question-specific ('Multiply every term inside the bracket by the term outside', for-student-example.md:43) — specific and task-focused, which is what the feedback literature asks for. The problem is quantity and placement, not kind.

Positive marking is baked in (SKILL.md:61-67: benefit of the doubt, method marks stand through slips, SC and ft applied), so working on the page is rewarded — the same message the tutor skill gives her ('blanks score zero but working scores method marks', maths-tutor-session/SKILL.md:69).

The skill already knows blanks are the behavioural metric (SKILL.md:147: 'Blanks per paper are the tracked behavioural metric and should be falling toward zero') and already raises the timing-versus-knowledge question (SKILL.md:84). The insight exists; only its placement in the student file is wrong.

The Spanish skill's range-versus-accuracy diagnosis (SKILL.md:157-161: 'the remedies are opposite') and its time-frame count (106-107: 'often the single cheapest mark to recover') are the two most actionable pieces of feedback in either skill — binary, memorable, and tied to a concrete change in behaviour. They need routing to the student, not rewriting.
Spanish marks meaning, not spelling, in English-language answers (SKILL.md:83-85) — a generous, spec-faithful rule that will not punish a slip.

The intro sentence of the student example explains why the answers are withheld ('so you can go back and work them out yourself', for-student-example.md:12) — transparent and respectful; keep a version of it.

The tracker's attempt page already derives 'Marks by topic, ordered by marks lost' (php/lib/dashboard.php:508-525) from the logged rows, and logs a neutral `question` cue per row (SKILL.md:120-121), so a shorter student view can be generated from data the system already holds.
The README's design stance — own best against own, no streaks or badges — gives a ready-made rule for the one number the student file should ask her to beat: her own blank count.
Second-person voice throughout the student example; no third-person 'the student' language leaks in.

findings.title: Restructure the For-Student file: five short sections, 300-word cap, the grid and every caveat move to the teacher file
findings.problem: Line 80 specifies: "Include: a summary block (mark, %, grade, tier), a compact per-question marks grid, a 'where you lost marks — what to review' table giving the topic and a method hint only, never the answer, and a prioritised list of revision topics." The example that produces is 755 words: a summary block giving the same result three ways (49/80, ≈61%, Grade 4), a 43-cell marks grid laid out in three column-pairs (lines 16-33), a 17-row table of 315 words (lines 37-55), a five-item list (57-63) and a conditional closing paragraph (65). Everything sits at the same visual weight; nothing says what to do first. The grid carries no information she can act on: every part not in the lost-marks table scored full marks, and all 17 lost rows are zeros, so the grid is a longer restatement of the table beneath it.
findings.why_it_matters: Reviews of feedback (Hattie & Timperley 2007; Shute 2008) and the EEF's 2021 guidance report converge on feedback that is specific, task-focused, forward-looking and limited in quantity; Shute's guidelines say explicitly to present feedback in manageable units and not to overwhelm. ADHD adds working-memory and sustained-attention limits (Martinussen et al. 2005 meta-analysis on working memory in ADHD), so a two-screen document with three tables is most likely read as far as the grade line and closed. The parent's objective is engagement; the file should be the shortest thing that changes what she does next.
findings.proposal:
Replacement for SKILL.md line 80 (maths) and lines 147-150 (Spanish):

"- **`For-Student_<paper>-<series>.md`** — the copy handed to the student. One page, at most 300 words, in this order: (1) **What worked** — 2-4 bullets naming a question and the behaviour that earned the mark; (2) **Blanks** — count and marks, the skip-vs-time reading with question numbers, then the blank question numbers with a 3-6 word cue each and no hints; (3) **Next three things** — at most three actions, each starting with a verb, ordered by marks recoverable; (4) **Re-try list** — only the parts she attempted and lost marks on, at most eight rows: Q + cue + marks + a first-step hint of 15 words or fewer; (5) **Next session** — what it opens with and that re-tries will be checked; then, if the parent wants it, one plain line: 'Mark: 49/80. Grade on this paper: 4.' It must NOT contain the correct answers. Moves to the teacher file: the per-question marks grid, the percentage, the tier note, every boundary caveat and comparison, the topic-gap clusters beyond three, method hints for blank questions, and the 'secure topics' list. See examples/for-student-example.md."

Section caps: What worked ≤ 70 words · Blanks ≤ 80 words · Next three ≤ 75 words · Re-try list ≤ 8 rows / ≤ 120 words · Next session ≤ 40 words · grade line ≤ 12 words. Total ≤ 300 words (current example: 755).
findings.evidence_needed: Quantity-limited, task-focused written feedback improves subsequent performance in adolescents (Hattie & Timperley 2007 review; Shute 2008 review; Kluger & DeNisi 1996 meta-analysis; EEF 2021 guidance); working-memory limits in ADHD (Martinussen et al. 2005 meta-analysis).

findings.title: The grade is the first thing she reads, is given and taken away in the same line, and comes with a ceiling
findings.problem: Line 9: "| **Grade** | **Grade 4** (a strong 3 / low 4 on today's tougher marking) |" and line 10: "| **Note** | This paper is Foundation, so the highest possible grade is 5. |". These are the first two substantive lines of her sheet. The hedge is inherited from the reference's instruction (line 71) to "report both" grades for pre-2023 papers — right for the parent, but in the student file the grade is awarded and then downgraded in one breath, 'tougher marking' tells her the number was inflated, and a ceiling ('highest possible grade is 5') is stated before a word about what she did. Line 98 of the skill itself calls a single paper 'a noisy estimate' — the noise is her headline.
findings.why_it_matters: Butler (1988, experiment with 11-12-year-olds): pupils given grades plus comments performed no better than pupils given grades alone and lost interest, while comments alone improved performance — grades wash out the comments beneath them. Kluger & DeNisi (1996, meta-analysis of 607 effects) found feedback that draws attention to the self rather than the task lowers or reverses its effect. For a 13-year-old sitting two years early, a grade label is maximally self-referential, and a hedged one invites the reading 'really a 3'.
findings.proposal: Delete rows 8-10 of the summary block. The student file opens with 'Your mark: 49 / 80' and nothing else numeric. If the parent wants a grade shown, it is one plain line after the actions: 'Grade on this paper: 4.' No hedge, no tier note, no percentage. Add to Step 6 after line 98: "The two-grade comparison, the tier ceiling, the notional paper boundary and the percentage are for the teacher file only. The student file states one grade, once, without a hedge, after the actions — or none for a single paper if the parent prefers; ask once and remember." Add to gcse-grading-standards.md line 71 after 'report both': '(in the teacher file; the student file carries one grade at most)'.
findings.evidence_needed: Grades alongside comments suppress the effect of comments (Butler 1988 experiment); self-directed versus task-directed feedback (Kluger & DeNisi 1996 meta-analysis).

findings.why_it_matters: Mueller & Dweck (1998, experiments with 10-12-year-olds): praise for process sustains persistence after subsequent failure; praise for the person or outcome reduces it. Hattie & Timperley rank task- and process-level feedback most effective and person-level praise least. Her logs show working omitted twice on 2 Sep even when asked for; a marked paper is the natural place to show her the marks that working earned.

Without a rule, each marking run will re-invent the tone, and the example file is the only thing holding it — and the example is the problem.
findings.proposal:
### Writing the student file — rules (add verbatim to both marker skills)

The student file is read by a 13-year-old on her own. It is the shortest thing that changes what she does next, not a record. Rules:

1. **One page. At most 300 words, five sections, three actions, and no table longer than eight rows.** If it is longer, move detail to the teacher file — never to a smaller font or a denser table.
2. **Open with what worked, as behaviour.** Two to four bullets, each naming a question and the thing she did that earned the mark: "you wrote the first step before the answer", "you gave both forms", "you tried every question up to 17a". Never a trait: no "clever", "natural", "good at", "talented", "brilliant". Allowed verbs: you wrote, you checked, you showed, you tried, you kept going.
3. **Blanks get their own section, counted, before the wrong answers.** State the number of blank parts and the marks they were worth, next to the marks lost to wrong answers. Read the pattern before you name it: blanks followed by full-mark answers later in the paper are skips, not time — say which, with the question numbers. A blank gets a "first line you could have written", never a method hint: she never tried it, so there is nothing to correct. Use the tutor's words: "what's one thing you could write down?"
4. **At most three next actions, each starting with a verb she can do in under fifteen minutes without help.** "Re-try 17b and 28 without looking, then ask Claude to check them." Never "revise", "practise", "work on", "focus on", "look at". Order by marks recoverable. Anything beyond three goes to the teacher file's gap list.
5. **Hints are first steps, never last steps.** Fifteen words or fewer, starting with an imperative ("Write", "Multiply", "Put"), naming only the first thing to write. If one step remains after your hint, it is an answer — move it to the teacher file.
6. **Every question reference carries a cue and its marks.** "17b — expanding a bracket (2)", never a bare "17b". Take the cue from the `question` text you log to the tracker; that text must itself contain no answer.
7. **The grade is one plain line at the end, or absent.** State the grade on the paper's own boundaries once, with no hedge. Percentage, tier ceiling, notional paper boundaries, the restored-standards comparison and any "strong 3 / low 4" phrasing belong in the teacher file only. For a single paper, ask the parent once whether she wants a grade shown at all and remember the answer.
8. **Ask, don't diagnose, about time.** Where blanks cluster at the back, end with one question for her to answer with her parent: "Did the time run out, or did you stop?" Never tell her to "practise pacing".
9. **Close with the next session, not a topic list.** One or two sentences: what the next session opens with, and that anything she re-tries before then will be checked.
10. **Voice.** Second person, present tense, sentences under twenty words. No exam-board register anywhere in the student file: no M1/A1/B1, ft, SC, AO2, band, tier, boundary, series, notional. "Marks" and "questions" are the only technical words she needs.
11. **Compare only with her own last paper, and only where it moved the right way** ("last paper 7 blanks, this paper 3"). Never with a target grade, a boundary, or the exam date.
12. **Read it back as her.** Before saving, reread the file asking: what is the first thing she does after reading this? If the honest answer is "closes it", cut until it isn't.
findings.evidence_needed: Brief, specific, positively framed feedback for pupils with ADHD (DuPaul & Stoner — expert/guideline level; a stronger source is needed); consistency of feedback register (no direct study; consensus).

findings.problem: Lines 147-150 are the whole specification: "handed to the student. It must NOT contain the correct answers or model translations … Include the summary, a per-question marks grid, a 'where you lost marks' table giving the grammar point and a hint only, and a prioritised revision list." No example, so every run invents the format. Band-marked work has its own failure modes: (a) a 90-word essay with a dozen minor errors becomes a 12-row table of grammar slips; (b) descriptor language ('communication mostly clear with occasional lapses', 'AO2 band 4') leaks from the justification the skill rightly demands at line 97-99 into her file; (c) the range-or-accuracy verdict (158-161: 'the remedies are opposite: range is fixed by learning structures, accuracy by slowing down and checking verbs') and the time-frame count (106-107: 'often the single cheapest mark to recover') are addressed to the marker and never routed to her; (d) the progress-tracker appendix names her Spanish behavioural metrics as translation elements attempted and time-frame range, and the student file has no place for either.
findings.why_it_matters: The range/accuracy verdict is strategy-level feedback of the kind that changes behaviour (slow down and check verbs, or learn two structures) and it is binary and memorable — the ideal single takeaway for a student who will not read a table. Written corrective feedback research in second-language writing (Bitchener & Knoch; Ellis et al.) finds focused correction of a few forms more effective than unfocused correction of everything, which argues directly against a row per slip.

- **Her two numbers are time frames used and translation pieces that got across** — not blanks. Report both as plain counts with the next step attached: "Time frames: 2 of 3 — add one sentence about what you will do." / "Translation: 11 of 15 pieces got across."
- **At most three grammar points, each with a count.** "Preterite -er endings (wrong ×3)", never fifteen rows of individual slips. Cluster by grammar point first; a theme is never a row.

findings.title: Hints range from 3 to 32 words with no rule: some are the whole method, one is a step from the answer, and several say 'revise' with nothing to do
findings.problem: Line 42: "Revise the equation of a **horizontal** line." — no action she can take now. Line 47: "Read it straight from y = mx + **c**." — for a question she left blank, she may not know that form. Line 40 (9a) is 32 words and the entire method. Line 51: "Rearrange 4y = 5x into y = ▢x, then turn the multiplier into a percentage." — one step from the answer (the box is 1.25) and arguably breaches line 82's rule that a hint 'is fine' only while the answer is not written. Line 40's 'Recheck how many hours are left for the last day' tells her where her error was, which is good, but the rest of the row solves it for her.
findings.why_it_matters: A hint that carries the whole route removes the retrieval work the separation rule exists to preserve (testing effect, Roediger & Karpicke 2006). A hint that says 'revise' gives an ADHD student nothing to initiate on. Specific means 'names the first thing to write', not 'complete'.
findings.proposal: Rule (in the shared block, item 5): fifteen words or fewer; starts with an imperative; names the first step only; if one step remains after the hint it is an answer and moves to the teacher file; never 'revise', 'look at', 'practise'. Rewrites for the example: 10d → "Write down what y equals at every point on a flat line."; 9a → "Start by writing the four fixed days' hours as one sum."; 24 → "Get y on its own first, then decide which one you are comparing to."; 19b → "Find the number standing on its own at the end of the equation."; 18b → "Write both percentages first, then divide both by the smaller one." (the last is a first step, not the route to 4.25).
findings.evidence_needed: Retrieval practice / testing effect (Roediger & Karpicke 2006 experiments); specificity without completeness in hints (Shute 2008 review).

findings.problem: The skills send the worked answers to the tracker's per-question `note` — the teacher example logs notes like "Correct route: (100−68)/2=16, so 68:16=4.25:1", "6/120×500=25" and "10x−5=6x+9 → 4x=14 → x=3.5". render_attempt prints the 'Answer given' and 'Note' columns for every question in an always-open table (lines 492-506), so the attempt page is the answer key the two-file rule exists to withhold. The dashboard is public unless DASHBOARD_PUBLIC=false, and the README says the Spanish practice board on the same host is 'the reason she keeps playing'; from there the kicker goes to /s/spanish, the index, /s/maths, then a large '148/240 ≈ grade below 4' badge (372-377) that links to the attempt. What she would see: a header reading '≈ grade below 4 on tier F' (the seeded F table stops at grade 4, so anything under 157/240 is 'below 4' even though the reference at gcse-grading-standards.md:34 gives June 2024 grade 3 = 117, and 148 ≥ 117); '7 left blank'; a 43-row table with 17 red-bordered rows before any statement of what went right; and 'Marks by topic — ordered by marks lost' at the bottom.
findings.why_it_matters: Two things: the separation rule the skills enforce carefully in files is undone one click away, so re-working a paper stops being retrieval practice the moment she finds the page; and the page as rendered is a wall of red under a 'below 4' label, the inverse of the structure proposed in finding 1. 'Below 4' is also simply wrong as a label for a 61.7% Foundation paper once the full table is stored.
findings.proposal: (a) S: in render_attempt, move the 'Marks by topic' block above the per-question table and wrap the table in `<details><summary>Question by question — marker notes include the answers</summary>…</details>`, closed by default; the parent pays one click, and a casual view shows totals and topics only. (b) S: seed.php:124 → `'F' => [[5, 186], [4, 157], [3, 117], [2, 77], [1, 37]]` (June 2024 Foundation, already in the reference) so gradeFor never returns 'below 4' for a scored paper; the badge and header then read '≈ grade 3'. (c) M, optional: a `?view=student` on the attempt route that renders the finding-1 sections from the logged rows (question cue, marks, blanks, topic refs are all already stored) and hides 'Answer given', 'Note' and the grade line — a student view is derivable without a schema change. (d) Skill rule for both markers under Step 7/9: "The `question` field is the one column safe to show her; it must be a neutral cue with no answer content. Answers and working belong only in `note`."
findings.evidence_needed: None for (a), (b), (d) — they follow from the skills' own separation rule and the reference's own boundary table. (c) rests on the same evidence as finding 1.

findings.title: Timing is asked of her as a self-diagnosis with an undoable action, and nothing at input time records whether the sitting was timed or finished
findings.where: /root/.claude/skills/synced/4573a9f7-2a0f-468d-a55f-752a46b4cb7c_a7c9a5f9-6655-41a2-821b-3115c7ffaf84/gcse-maths-marker/examples/for-student-example.md line 65; /root/.claude/skills/synced/4573a9f7-2a0f-468d-a55f-752a46b4cb7c_a7c9a5f9-6655-41a2-821b-3115c7ffaf84/gcse-maths-marker/SKILL.md lines 30-38 (Inputs to gather first) and 84; the paper `note` field shown at /home/user/education-study-tracker/php/lib/dashboard.php lines 472-474
findings.problem: Line 65: "If you ran out of time rather than got stuck, practising your timing/pacing will pick up easy marks next time." It asks her to decide a distinction the marker could not make, and offers 'practising your timing/pacing' — not something a 13-year-old can go and do. The Inputs section asks for the paper, the scheme and the answers, but never whether the paper was sat under time, whether she finished, or where she was when time ran out; the logged attempt records a blank count but not the conditions, so the progress tracker's behavioural metric cannot distinguish 'did not know' from 'ran out' or, per finding 3, from 'skipped'.
findings.why_it_matters: The blanks metric is the only behavioural measure the system holds; without sitting conditions it conflates three states with three different remedies (teach, pace, attempt). For her, one question with two concrete answers she can give to her parent is actionable; 'practise pacing' is not.
findings.proposal: (a) Add a fourth input at SKILL.md line 37: "4. **Sitting conditions** — was it timed, did she finish, and if not, the last question reached and minutes left. Ask the parent; if unknown, say so rather than inferring it from the blanks." Record it in the paper `note`: 'timed 90 min, finished with 5 min left' / 'untimed, stopped at 26'. (b) Replace line 65 with: "**One question for you:** 27 and 28 are the only blanks that look like time. Did the time run out, or did you stop? Tell [parent] which — it changes what we practise next." (c) When the parent's answer is known, state it as fact instead: "You ran out of time at 27. Those two questions were worth 8 marks; next paper we practise moving on after two minutes stuck and coming back." (d) The progress-tracker report's behavioural line then reads blanks split by cause.
findings.evidence_needed: Recording sitting conditions is a measurement fix, not a research claim. Time-perception and pacing difficulties in ADHD (e.g. Barkley, Murphy & Bush 2001 on time estimation in ADHD — needs confirmation) would justify treating 'ran out' as a distinct, coachable state.

findings.title: Every question is a bare number, forcing a three-way cross-reference (sheet, paper, her script) that the tracker log already has the cue text to avoid
findings.where: /root/.claude/skills/synced/4573a9f7-2a0f-468d-a55f-752a46b4cb7c_a7c9a5f9-6655-41a2-821b-3115c7ffaf84/gcse-maths-marker/examples/for-student-example.md lines 16-33 and 37-55; /root/.claude/skills/synced/4573a9f7-2a0f-468d-a55f-752a46b4cb7c_a7c9a5f9-6655-41a2-821b-3115c7ffaf84/gcse-maths-marker/SKILL.md lines 120-121 (the `question` cue is already required in the log)
findings.problem: Rows read '17b | Expanding brackets | …' and the grid places '19c' in the third column-pair of a 43-cell table. To use the sheet she needs the paper open and her script beside it; the log already carries a neutral cue per question ('Factorise 6x²+8x', line 121) that never reaches her.
findings.why_it_matters: Split-attention across three documents is a working-memory cost (Sweller's split-attention effect; Martinussen et al. 2005 on working memory in ADHD), and for a home-educated student the paper may not be to hand when she reads the sheet — the sheet then does nothing until it is.
findings.proposal: Rule (shared block, item 6): every reference is 'Q + 3-6 word cue + marks', taken from the logged `question` field: "17b — expanding a bracket (2)", "27 — Pythagoras then area (5)". The cue must contain no answer content, because it is also the one column the tracker can safely show her (finding 9d).
findings.evidence_needed: Split-attention effect (Sweller, cognitive load theory — general population); working memory in ADHD (Martinussen et al. 2005 meta-analysis).

findings.title: The file ends without saying what happens next or whether re-tries will be checked — close with the next session, not a list
findings.where: /root/.claude/skills/synced/4573a9f7-2a0f-468d-a55f-752a46b4cb7c_a7c9a5f9-6655-41a2-821b-3115c7ffaf84/gcse-maths-marker/examples/for-student-example.md lines 57-65 (ends with a topic list and a conditional); /root/.claude/skills/synced/4573a9f7-2a0f-468d-a55f-752a46b4cb7c_a7c9a5f9-6655-41a2-821b-3115c7ffaf84/gcse-maths-marker/SKILL.md Step 7 lines 153-156 (hand-off to gcse-progress-tracker); cf. /root/.claude/skills/synced/4573a9f7-2a0f-468d-a55f-752a46b4cb7c_a7c9a5f9-6655-41a2-821b-3115c7ffaf84/maths-tutor-session/SKILL.md lines 57-62 (a session opens with a retrieval starter that could be named here)
findings.problem: The sheet tells her the answers are withheld 'so you can go back and work them out yourself' (line 12) but never says what to do with what she works out, or when. Hattie & Timperley's 'where to next?' is answered with topic names. From her side, re-trying a question is either checked at some point or pointless, and the file does not say which.
findings.why_it_matters: Feedback is formative only when the loop closes (feedback → action → check; Wiliam). For ADHD a known near-term checkpoint is a stronger prompt to start than an open-ended instruction, and it is the difference between the sheet being a task and being a verdict.
findings.proposal: Final section 'Next session' (≤ 40 words): "Your next maths session starts with 17b and 28. If you re-try them before then, bring what you wrote — Claude will check it against the marker's copy. Nothing else to prepare." Rule: the marker takes 'what it opens with' from the progress-tracker hand-off (Step 7) or tracker_review_queue's planned-next so the sentence is true, and the tutor skill's starter honours it.
findings.evidence_needed: Closing the feedback loop as the condition for formative effect (Wiliam 2011, Embedded Formative Assessment — expert/review); 'where to next' (Hattie & Timperley 2007).

findings.title: The teacher file has no debrief script, so how the sheet is handed over is left to the moment
findings.where: /root/.claude/skills/synced/4573a9f7-2a0f-468d-a55f-752a46b4cb7c_a7c9a5f9-6655-41a2-821b-3115c7ffaf84/gcse-maths-marker/examples/for-teacher-example.md lines 66-82 (topic gaps, secure list, timing flag, tracker link); /root/.claude/skills/synced/4573a9f7-2a0f-468d-a55f-752a46b4cb7c_a7c9a5f9-6655-41a2-821b-3115c7ffaf84/gcse-spanish-marker/SKILL.md lines 143-146
findings.problem: The teacher file ends with the gap list, the provisional-marks note and the tracker link. The parent 'oversees and sometimes runs or reviews sessions' and will usually be the person who hands over the student file; nothing tells them what to say first, what to ask, or when to stop. The system brief records that two full sessions were run on 2 Sep and that frustration handling lives only in the tutor skill (line 74) — a marked paper is the highest-stakes moment for that.
findings.why_it_matters: Parent-delivered feedback for adolescents with ADHD works better when it is brief, starts positive and ends with a single agreed next step (Family–School Success and related parent-involvement interventions, Power et al. 2012 RCT); a three-line script costs nothing and makes the handover consistent across papers and parents.
findings.proposal: Add to the end of both teacher-file templates a section 'Handing this over (≤ 60 words)': "Read 'What worked' aloud first. Then ask the one question in the sheet and write her answer in the tracker note. Agree which of the three next things she will do and when — one, not three. Stop there; the re-try list is for her own time. If she is upset by the blank count, leave the sheet and come back tomorrow."
findings.evidence_needed: Parent-mediated academic support for adolescents with ADHD (Power et al. 2012 Family–School Success RCT; Sibley et al. on parent–teen interventions — need confirmation of applicability to feedback handover).
